result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.maximum_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute maximum flow from source to sink. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.maximum_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Compute maximum flow from source to sink. title: >- [Graph.maximum_flow()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute maximum flow from source to sink. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute maximum flow from source to sink. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L64299-L64455){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.maximum_flow( source, target, capacity=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum flow](../assets/graphs/maximum-flow.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed network from source S to sink T through A and B. Each edge is labeled flow over capacity, and every edge carries flow, drawn in the accent color with width growing with the flow. The card lists the flow per edge, which totals 5." width="100%"} Finds the maximum amount of flow that can be sent from the source node to the sink node through the network. Uses the Edmonds-Karp algorithm (Ford-Fulkerson with BFS), which guarantees `O(VE²)` time complexity. Each edge has a capacity, the most flow it can carry. With the default `capacity=None`, an edge's capacity is taken from its `capacity` attribute if it has one, otherwise from its weight on a weighted graph, and otherwise it is `1.0`. You can also name a custom capacity attribute. Parallel edges between the same two nodes add to the total capacity between them, but each keeps its own capacity and reports its own flow. Self-loops carry no flow. Maximum flow models how much of something can move through a network with limited link capacities, for example: - throughput of a pipeline, power grid, or transport network - bandwidth available between two hosts in a communication network - assignment and matching problems that reduce to flow (e.g. bipartite matching) On a directed graph flow only moves along edge direction. On an undirected graph each edge can carry flow either way, and the value reported for it is the net flow. Several different flow assignments can achieve the same maximum; this method returns one of them. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the flow starts from, given as an integer node ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the flow ends at, given as an integer node ID or a string label. Must be a different node than `source=`. [capacity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as capacity. Every edge must hold a numeric value for it (`"weight"` also accepts the edge weight of a weighted graph); otherwise a `ValueError` is raised. If `None` (default), each edge's `capacity` attribute is used when present, then its weight on weighted graphs, and `1.0` otherwise. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping `edge_id -> flow amount` for edges with positive flow. Edges that carry no flow are omitted, so the dictionary is empty when the sink is unreachable. Use `maximum_flow_value()` if you only need the total flow value. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or sink doesn't exist, they're the same node, any capacity is negative, or an edge lacks the attribute named by `capacity=`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Edmonds-Karp variant of Ford-Fulkerson is used: at each step it augments along the *shortest* augmenting path (measured in edge count) found by BFS, which bounds the total number of augmentations by $O(V \cdot E)$ and gives an $O(V \cdot E^2)$ overall runtime regardless of the actual capacities. Undirected edges are internally treated as antiparallel pairs with equal capacity, and self-loops carry no flow. The max-flow min-cut theorem guarantees that the total flow equals the capacity of the minimum $s$-$t$ cut; with unit capacities that is the edge count reported by `minimum_cut_value()`. Use `maximum_flow_value()` when only the number is needed. ## Examples {.doc-examples} With weighted edges acting as capacities, the flow algorithm finds how much can be routed from `S` to `T`, splitting across parallel paths as needed. Mapping edge IDs back to endpoint labels shows how much each edge carries: ::: {#1a49daa0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) .add_nodes( [ "S", # source "A", "B", "T", # sink ] ) .add_edges( [ ("S", "A", 10.0), ("S", "B", 5.0), ("A", "B", 15.0), ("A", "T", 10.0), ("B", "T", 10.0), ] ) ) flow = graph.maximum_flow("S", "T") label = graph.get_label_from_id { (label(graph.get_edge(eid).source), label(graph.get_edge(eid).target)): amount for eid, amount in sorted(flow.items()) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {('S', 'A'): 10.0, ('S', 'B'): 5.0, ('A', 'T'): 10.0, ('B', 'T'): 5.0} ``` ::: ::: Summing the flow on the edges leaving the source gives the total, which matches `maximum_flow_value()`: ::: {#cc8e6386 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} s_id = graph.get_id_from_label("S") total = sum(amount for eid, amount in flow.items() if graph.get_edge(eid).source == s_id) total, graph.maximum_flow_value("S", "T") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (15.0, 15.0) ``` ::: ::: You can use any numeric edge attribute as capacity instead of weight, which is useful when weight already represents something else (like distance). Here the `A -> B -> C` route is limited to 50 by its second edge, and the direct `A -> C` edge adds another 30: ::: {#5865602e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"bandwidth": 100}), ("B", "C", {"bandwidth": 50}), ("A", "C", {"bandwidth": 30}), ] ) ) graph.maximum_flow("A", "C", capacity="bandwidth") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {2: 50.0, 3: 30.0, 1: 50.0} ``` ::: ::: For unweighted graphs, every edge has capacity `1.0`, so max flow equals the number of edge-disjoint paths. Both routes `S -> A -> T` and `S -> B -> T` are used, and each of the four edges carries `1.0`: ::: {#6d8672d2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_edges([("S", "A"), ("S", "B"), ("A", "T"), ("B", "T")], auto_create_nodes=True) ) graph.maximum_flow("S", "T") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {3: 1.0, 1: 1.0, 4: 1.0, 2: 1.0} ``` ::: :::
